set.detail: Trajan's Column was dedicated on 12 May 113 (Fasti Ostienses) in a small court between the two libraries of the Forum of Trajan, behind the Basilica Ulpia. Built of 17 drums of Luna marble, 29.8 m high (100 Roman feet) on a pedestal, about 38 m with the base, it carries a continuous spiral frieze about 200 m long, winding 23 times around the shaft, with some 2,600 figures in 155 scenes narrating the two Dacian wars (101-102 and 105-106), separated by a figure of Victory writing on a shield. The narrative begins with the crossing of the Danube on a pontoon bridge watched by the river god and continues with marching, building camps, roads and bridges, sacrifices, speeches (adlocutiones), battles, sieges, the submission of Dacian chiefs, Trajan's bridge at Drobeta, the storming of Sarmizegetusa, the Dacians' poisoning themselves and finally the suicide of Decebalus as Roman cavalrymen reach him, and the deportation of the Dacians. Trajan appears some 58 times. The frieze shows far more construction work than fighting, an image of the army as an instrument of order. The designer is often thought to be Apollodorus of Damascus. The column's height, according to the dedication inscription (whose letters became the model for Roman capitals), showed how deep the hill had been cut to make room for the forum, though this reading is debated. A spiral staircase of 185 steps inside, lit by small windows, leads to the top, where a bronze statue of Trajan stood (replaced by St Peter in 1587). Trajan's ashes and those of Plotina were placed in a golden urn in the pedestal, an exception to the ban on burial within the pomerium. The frieze is a key source for Roman military equipment, though its depiction of legionaries in segmented armour and auxiliaries in mail is partly conventional. Its sources may have been Trajan's lost commentaries on the war (Dacica). The relief could not have been read easily from the ground; it may have been viewed from the library terraces. It inspired the Column of Marcus Aurelius and, much later, Napoleon's column in the Place Vendome.
set.debate: Meaning of the inscription's statement about the height of the hill removed, and how the frieze was meant to be viewed.

set.detail: After failing to take Hatra in 117 and with his eastern conquests in revolt, Trajan, now 63 and in poor health, left Antioch for Rome, leaving Hadrian in command of the army in Syria. He suffered a stroke that left him partly paralysed and developed oedema, and died at Selinus in Cilicia (renamed Traianopolis) on or about 8 August 117. Plotina, his niece Matidia, the praetorian prefect Attianus and the household were with him. The circumstances of Hadrian's succession were controversial from the start. Hadrian, Trajan's cousin once removed and husband of his grand-niece Sabina, had been consul in 108, governor of Syria and evidently favoured, but had not been formally adopted or given the title Caesar. On 9 August Hadrian at Antioch received letters announcing his adoption, and on 11 August news of Trajan's death, which he celebrated as his dies imperii. Dio, citing his father Apronianus, a later governor of Cilicia, reports that the adoption was a fiction arranged by Plotina, who concealed Trajan's death for several days and had someone impersonate his weak voice behind a curtain; the Historia Augusta repeats rumours that Trajan intended to leave the choice to the Senate or even to name Neratius Priscus. A recently noticed detail is that the letters announcing the adoption were signed by Plotina, not Trajan, and that Trajan's chamberlain Phaedimus died suddenly days later. Whatever the truth, the Syrian army acclaimed Hadrian, and the Senate accepted him. Trajan's ashes were taken to Rome by Plotina and Matidia and placed in his column; he was deified and celebrated with a posthumous Parthian triumph, his image carried in the procession. His reign was remembered as the empire's zenith: the Senate later wished new emperors to be "luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan" (felicior Augusto, melior Traiano). Hadrian immediately abandoned Mesopotamia and Assyria and executed four consular generals in 118, which poisoned his relations with the Senate.
set.debate: Whether Trajan really adopted Hadrian or Plotina staged the adoption after his death.

set.detail: The Pantheon standing today was built under Hadrian, probably between about 114 and 125, on the site of Agrippa's temple of 25 BC, which had burned in 80, been restored by Domitian and burned again in 110. Brick stamps date most of the fabric to 115-125, suggesting the project may have been started under Trajan, perhaps by Apollodorus. Hadrian reinstated Agrippa's original inscription on the porch frieze (M AGRIPPA L F COS TERTIVM FECIT), in keeping with his policy of not putting his own name on buildings he restored, which led scholars until the nineteenth century to date the building to Agrippa. The building combines a pedimented porch of sixteen monolithic granite columns (the front eight of grey Mons Claudianus granite, each 11.8 m and weighing about 60 tonnes; the planned 50-foot columns apparently could not be obtained, so the porch is lower than the intermediate block, producing an awkward junction) with a rotunda whose interior diameter and height are both 43.3 m, so that a sphere would fit exactly inside. The unreinforced concrete dome, still the largest of its kind in the world, rests on walls 6 m thick and is lightened by graded aggregates: heavy travertine and tuff at the bottom, then brick, and light pumice and scoria near the top, with 140 coffers and an open oculus 8.9 m across. Hidden relieving arches in the drum distribute the load. The interior was paved and revetted with coloured marbles from Egypt, Numidia and Phrygia. Its function is debated: Dio says the name came from the statues of many gods or the resemblance of the dome to the heavens, and that Hadrian held court there; it may have been a dynastic shrine as much as a temple. The sun's disc entering through the oculus moves around the interior, and on 21 April, Rome's birthday, its noon beam strikes the entrance, possibly by design. Septimius Severus and Caracalla restored it in 202, and in 609 Pope Boniface IV consecrated it as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres, which saved it. Its bronze roof tiles were stripped by Constans II in 663 and the porch bronzes by Urban VIII in 1625.
set.debate: Whether begun under Trajan; function as temple, dynastic hall or audience hall.

set.detail: Hadrian visited Britain in 122 and, according to the Historia Augusta, "was the first to build a wall 80 miles long to separate the Romans from the barbarians". The work was directed by the governor Aulus Platorius Nepos, who came from Lower Germany with legio VI Victrix, and carried out by the three British legions (II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix), whose building inscriptions survive. The original plan provided for a stone wall 10 Roman feet wide from Newcastle to the Irthing and a turf wall 20 feet wide from there to Bowness-on-Solway, with a ditch in front, small fortlets every Roman mile (milecastles) with gates, and two turrets between each. Before completion the plan changed: the stone wall was narrowed to 8 feet or less (the "narrow wall" on "broad foundations" seen at several sites), and some sixteen forts were added on the line itself, such as Housesteads, Chesters and Birdoswald, moving the garrison from the Stanegate road behind onto the wall. Behind the wall a great earthwork known as the Vallum, a flat-bottomed ditch with mounds on either side, marked the southern edge of the military zone. The wall was extended east to Wallsend and supplemented by forts and towers along the Cumbrian coast. The wall's purpose is debated: a military barrier against attack, a means of controlling movement and taxing trade through the milecastle gates, a statement of imperial power, or all of these; its forts housed auxiliary units, not legions, and it was not designed for fighting from the top. The Vindolanda tablets, written in the years just before the wall, mention the "Brittunculi" (wretched little Britons). Construction took about six years for the main elements. The Antonine Wall superseded it from 142, but it was recommissioned around 158-160 and remained the frontier, with modifications, until the end of Roman Britain. The Staffordshire Moorlands pan, a souvenir bronze vessel naming four western forts, and the Rudge cup show that it was perceived as a monument in antiquity. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1987.
set.debate: Purpose: defensive barrier, customs and control line or symbolic statement.

set.detail: The second great Jewish revolt broke out in 132 in Judaea under Shimon bar Kosiba, whom followers called Bar Kokhba ("son of the star", after Numbers 24.17) and opponents later Bar Koziba ("son of the lie"). Its causes are debated. Dio says it was provoked by Hadrian's foundation of the colony of Aelia Capitolina on the ruins of Jerusalem with a temple of Jupiter on the site of the Temple; the Historia Augusta claims it was a ban on circumcision, which Hadrian may have extended to Jews as part of a general prohibition on castration and mutilation. Eusebius dates Aelia's foundation after the war. The revolt was well prepared: Dio says the Jews had deliberately made defective weapons for the Romans so that they would be rejected and kept, and had built a network of underground hideouts, many of which have been found in the Judaean foothills. The rebels controlled much of Judaea, though probably not Jerusalem itself, and issued coins overstruck on Roman denarii and tetradrachms with legends "Year one of the redemption of Israel", "For the freedom of Israel" and images of the Temple facade. Bar Kosiba bore the title "nasi (prince) of Israel", and the priest Eleazar appears beside him on coins. Rabbi Akiva reputedly hailed him as the messiah, to which Yohanan ben Torta replied "Akiva, grass will grow from your cheeks and the son of David will still not have come." Christians who refused to support him were persecuted, according to Justin Martyr. The governor Tineius Rufus and the legate of Syria, Publicius Marcellus, could not contain the rising; legio XXII Deiotariana may have been destroyed. Hadrian summoned Sextus Julius Severus from Britain and drew troops from at least a dozen legions; the war lasted until 135 or 136 and ended with the fall of Betar. Hadrian himself seems to have been present for a time and omitted the customary formula "I and the army are well" in his report to the Senate, a sign of heavy losses. Hadrian took a second imperatorial acclamation, and Severus and others received triumphal ornaments.
set.debate: Cause (Aelia Capitolina or the circumcision ban) and whether the rebels held Jerusalem; the fate of XXII Deiotariana.

set.detail: Shortly after his accession Antoninus Pius ordered an advance into southern Scotland, and his governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus, after campaigns in 139-142, built a new frontier across the Forth-Clyde isthmus, about 160 km north of Hadrian's Wall. The Antonine Wall ran 37 Roman miles (about 60 km) from Bo'ness (Carriden) on the Forth to Old Kilpatrick on the Clyde. Unlike Hadrian's Wall it was built of turf on a stone foundation about 14 Roman feet wide, with a wide, deep ditch in front and a military road behind. The original plan seems to have had six large forts at roughly eight-mile intervals and fortlets every mile, but it was soon modified, with more forts added, giving some sixteen or seventeen at intervals of about two miles, such as Rough Castle, Bar Hill and Bearsden. Building was carried out by detachments of the three British legions, which recorded the lengths they completed on finely carved distance slabs, some twenty of which survive, showing victory scenes, sacrifices and bound captives. The Bridgeness slab depicts the suovetaurilia sacrifice. The wall was an expression of Antoninus's need for military prestige as much as of strategic necessity; he took his only imperatorial acclamation for the British victory, and Fronto compared the achievement to a triumph won by an emperor who stayed at home. Hadrian's Wall was partly decommissioned, its milecastle gates removed and the Vallum crossed. The occupation of the Antonine Wall was short. Much of the evidence once taken to indicate two periods of occupation with an interruption c. 155-158 has been reinterpreted, and the current view is that it was abandoned in the early 160s, at the start of Marcus Aurelius's reign, when Hadrian's Wall was restored. Septimius Severus reoccupied some of its forts during his Scottish campaigns (208-211). The name "Grim's Dyke" was used for it in the Middle Ages. It became part of the "Frontiers of the Roman Empire" World Heritage Site in 2008.
set.debate: Date and sequence of abandonment; whether there were one or two periods of occupation.

set.detail: Antoninus Pius died on 7 March 161 at his villa at Lorium, having given the night watchword "aequanimitas" and ordered the golden statue of Fortuna, kept in the emperor's bedroom, to be moved to that of Marcus. Marcus Aurelius, Caesar since 139 and holder of tribunician power and proconsular imperium since 147, was the obvious successor and the Senate offered him sole rule. He insisted, however, that his adoptive brother Lucius, son of Hadrian's first intended heir Lucius Aelius, be made co-emperor with equal titles, Imperator Caesar Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus, while Marcus took the name Antoninus. This was the first time the empire was formally ruled by two Augusti with equal powers, though Marcus alone was pontifex maximus and held seniority, having one more tribunician year. The arrangement honoured Hadrian's original plan of 138, under which Antoninus had adopted both young men. The two emperors went to the praetorian camp, where Lucius addressed the troops and they promised a donative of 20,000 sesterces each, a large sum. Lucius was betrothed to Marcus's daughter Lucilla. The motives for the collegiality are debated: loyalty to Hadrian's wishes, the need for a second emperor to command in war, as soon happened when Lucius went to the East in 162, and the desire to avoid a rival. Ancient writers contrasted Marcus's philosophical austerity with Lucius's love of pleasure, though the Historia Augusta's life of Verus is largely hostile invention. The joint rule set a precedent for collegial emperorship that became normal in the third and fourth centuries (Severus and Caracalla, Valerian and Gallienus, the Tetrarchy). The birth of twin sons to Faustina on 31 August 161, one of whom was Commodus, appeared to secure the dynasty. Within months the empire faced crisis: the Parthian invasion of Armenia and defeat at Elegeia, the Tiber flood and famine, and unrest in Britain and on the Rhine.
set.debate: Motives for sharing power and the reliability of the Historia Augusta's portrait of Lucius.

set.detail: The Antonine Plague, which first appeared among Roman troops in Mesopotamia in 165-166, was the first known pandemic in the Roman empire. The ancient sources say that it broke out at Seleucia on the Tigris when soldiers opened a golden casket in a temple of Apollo, or in Babylonia, and it spread with the returning army through Syria and Asia Minor to Rome in 166, and to the armies on the Danube by 168-169, where it struck the forces gathered at Aquileia and carried off the praetorian prefect Furius Victorinus. Galen, who left Rome in 166 and was summoned to Aquileia in 168-169, describes symptoms of fever, vomiting, diarrhoea with black stools, and a black, dry rash that left scabs, which led most modern scholars to identify it as smallpox, though measles has been proposed. Outbreaks recurred over the next two decades; the worst attested was in 189, when Dio says 2,000 people often died in a day in Rome. Estimates of mortality vary enormously. Some historians (Gilliam, Bruun) have argued for limited effects; others, using papyri from Egyptian villages that show sudden declines in tax-payers (as at Soknopaiou Nesos, where the adult male population fell by a third or more), the fall in wages and land prices, the interruption of gold-mining tablets in Dacia, a gap in dated inscriptions and brick stamps, and the end of new building, argue for overall losses of 10% or more, possibly 20-25% in some places (Duncan-Jones, Harper). The plague contributed to the manpower crisis of the Marcomannic wars, when Marcus recruited slaves, gladiators and brigands, and to the settlement of barbarians on depopulated land. Lucian's Alexander shows the oracular verse inscribed on doors to ward it off, and inscriptions from Pergamum, Hierapolis and elsewhere record oracles of Apollo of Claros prescribing rituals. Some historians see it as the beginning of the end of the Roman "optimum" of demographic and economic growth, together with climate deterioration after the second century. Chinese sources record epidemics in the 160s and 170s, possibly related.
set.debate: Disease identity (smallpox most likely) and mortality, from minor losses to 20-25%.

set.detail: In 170, when Marcus had launched an offensive across the Danube that seems to have ended in a serious defeat with the loss of up to 20,000 men (Lucian's Alexander mentions such a loss), a coalition of Marcomanni and Quadi under the Marcomannic king Ballomar broke through the Danube frontier, devastated Noricum and Pannonia, crossed the Julian Alps and besieged Aquileia, the great city at the head of the Adriatic, and destroyed Opitergium (Oderzo). It was the first invasion of Italy by a foreign enemy since the Cimbri and Teutones nearly three centuries earlier, and caused panic. The praetorian prefect Macrinius Vindex was killed in battle around the same time, and Marcus Claudius Fronto, commanding Dacia and Upper Moesia, fell fighting the Germans and Iazyges. At about the same time the Costoboci swept south through the Balkans to Greece, sacking the sanctuary of Eleusis, and Moors invaded Baetica. Aquileia held out. It had been fortified in haste in 168-169 under the praetorian prefects as part of a defence system in the Julian Alps, the praetentura Italiae et Alpium, commanded by Quintus Antistius Adventus, whose career inscription survives. The invaders were driven out of Italy in 171 by forces under Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus, Marcus's new son-in-law, and Publius Helvius Pertinax, who caught them as they recrossed the Danube with booty and prisoners. Marcus then moved his headquarters to Carnuntum and began the campaigns of 172-175. The chronology of 170 is uncertain, partly because the sources (Dio's epitome, the Historia Augusta, Ammianus Marcellinus 29.6.1) are fragmentary, and some scholars place the invasion in 167 or 169. The episode shook the confidence of the Antonine age and led to the creation of the Italian legions II and III Italica and a new defensive policy. It is regarded by many historians as the first sign of the barbarian pressure that dominated the third century.

Marcus Aurelius died on 17 March 180, aged 58, at his headquarters on the Danube, at Vindobona (Vienna) according to Aurelius Victor or at Sirmium according to Tertullian, during his second German expedition. Dio says that his doctors, eager to please Commodus, hastened his death, a claim generally dismissed; the Historia Augusta describes a final illness, possibly the plague, during which he refused food and drink. On the sixth day, he summoned his friends and spoke of the vanity of things, and on the seventh, sending Commodus away for fear of infection, he gave the tribune the watchword "Go to the rising sun, for I am already setting." He had arranged the succession carefully: Commodus, aged eighteen, had been Caesar since 166 and co-Augustus since 177, the first emperor's son "born in the purple" to succeed his father since Titus. Marcus's choice of a biological heir over adoption has been criticised since antiquity, though no alternative was available without excluding his son. Marcus was deified at once; his ashes were placed in the Mausoleum of Hadrian. His reign had been dominated by war and disaster: the Parthian war (161-166), the plague, the Marcomannic wars, the revolt of Avidius Cassius and the death of Faustina. He nevertheless won a reputation as the ideal philosopher-king, sustained by his Meditations, twelve books of private Stoic reflections written in Greek during the campaigns, by his clemency to Cassius's supporters and by his endowment of philosophy chairs at Athens. Dio, who lived through the reign, said that with his death history descended "from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust". Modern historians acknowledge his conscientiousness while noting his persecution of Christians (Lyon, 177), his debasement of the coinage and his apparent intention to annex territory north of the Danube, abandoned by Commodus. The equestrian bronze statue on the Capitol, preserved because it was believed to represent Constantine, and the Column of Marcus Aurelius on the Campus Martius are the main monuments of his reign.
set.debate: Place of death (Vindobona or Sirmium) and the wisdom of choosing Commodus.

set.detail: Commodus was murdered on the night of 31 December 192, aged 31, on the eve of the day when he planned to enter the consulship dressed as a gladiator from the gladiators' barracks, and, according to Herodian, to have the consuls designate killed. The conspirators were his mistress Marcia, the chamberlain (cubicularius) Eclectus and the new praetorian prefect Quintus Aemilius Laetus, all of whom feared for their lives; Herodian has the boy Philocommodus find a writing tablet listing them for execution. Marcia gave Commodus poisoned wine or beef after his bath; when he vomited and seemed likely to recover, they sent in the athlete Narcissus, his wrestling partner, who strangled him in his bath. The conspirators announced that he had died of apoplexy and went at once to the house of the urban prefect Publius Helvius Pertinax, who had probably been forewarned, and took him to the praetorian camp, where he was hailed emperor after promising a donative of 12,000 sesterces. The Senate, meeting before dawn, declared Commodus an enemy of the state and ordered his statues thrown down and his name erased, with ritual chants recorded by the Historia Augusta ("Let the enemy of the fatherland be dragged with the hook"); Pertinax had him buried quietly in the Mausoleum of Hadrian, and Septimius Severus later deified him to legitimise his own claim to be Marcus's son. Commodus's last years had been marked by his identification with Hercules, coins showing him in the lion skin, the renaming of the months with his titles and of Rome as Colonia Commodiana, his appearances in the arena in which he killed animals from a raised platform and fought gladiators with wooden weapons, and executions of senators. Dio, an eyewitness, records that senators in the Colosseum had to chew laurel leaves to stop themselves laughing when Commodus waved the severed head of an ostrich at them. His murder ended the Antonine dynasty and opened the civil wars of 193, the "year of the five emperors". Narcissus was executed by Severus; Laetus and Eclectus were killed with Pertinax in March 193.
